terms.definition: A built-in, always-enabled Auto Scaling Group check that monitors the system-level status (instance status and system status) of each EC2 instance. Detects infrastructure-level failures only.
terms.example: If the physical host fails and the EC2 instance stops responding, the EC2 health check marks it Unhealthy and ASG replaces it.

terms.definition: An optional (but recommended) health check type where the Elastic Load Balancer probes a configured HTTP endpoint on each instance and checks for a valid response. Detects application-level failures.
terms.example: If your web server crashes inside the EC2 instance, the ELB health check detects it even though the instance itself is still running.

terms.definition: The number of seconds ASG waits after launching a new instance before starting health checks on it. Prevents premature termination during instance startup. Default is 300 seconds.
terms.example: If your application takes 3 minutes to boot, set the grace period to at least 240 seconds to avoid health check failures on perfectly fine instances.

terms.definition: A scaling policy that adds or removes a fixed number of instances when a CloudWatch alarm fires. Has a cooldown period during which no further scaling occurs. Best for demos and simple workloads.
terms.example: When CPU > 70%, always add exactly 2 instances.

terms.definition: A scaling policy that adds different numbers of instances based on how much the metric has exceeded the threshold. Uses instance warmup instead of a hard cooldown. Best for production.
terms.example: Add 1 instance for CPU 60-70%, add 2 for 70-85%, add 4 for above 85%.

terms.definition: A scaling policy where you set a target metric value and AWS automatically manages the instance count to maintain that target. Similar to a thermostat — you set the temperature, not the fan speed.
terms.example: Keep average CPU utilization at 50%. AWS adds or removes instances as needed to hit that target.

terms.definition: A scaling policy that adjusts min/max/desired capacity on a recurring schedule. Ideal for predictable, time-based traffic patterns.
terms.example: Every weekday at 8 AM, set minimum instances to 10. At 8 PM, reduce back to 2.

terms.definition: A scaling policy that uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively launch instances before demand arrives.
terms.example: If every Friday at 6 PM traffic triples, Predictive Scaling starts adding instances at 5:30 PM — before the spike hits.

terms.definition: The time (in seconds) after a Simple Scaling action during which no further scaling actions occur. Default is 300 seconds. Prevents rapid back-and-forth scaling.
terms.example: After adding 2 instances at T=0, the cooldown blocks any further scaling until T=300.

terms.definition: The time after a Step Scaling action during which newly launched instances are given to stabilize before contributing to CloudWatch metric aggregates. Does not block further scaling actions like a cooldown does.
terms.example: New instances are excluded from CPU average calculations during warmup so they don't artificially lower the metric.

terms.definition: A monitoring rule that watches a metric (like CPU utilization) and changes state (OK → ALARM) when the metric crosses a threshold. ALARM state can trigger Auto Scaling actions.
terms.example: Create an alarm: if average CPUUtilization > 70% for 5 minutes, go to ALARM state and trigger scale-out.

terms.definition: Also called Deregistration Delay. Allows in-flight requests to complete before an instance is removed from a Target Group. The Load Balancer stops sending new requests to the draining instance but lets existing ones finish. Range: 0–3600 seconds, default 300 seconds.
terms.example: A user uploading a file won't get a dropped connection just because ASG is terminating their instance — the upload completes within the drain window.

terms.definition: An Application Load Balancer feature that routes requests to different Target Groups based on the URL path. Core enabler of microservices architecture.
terms.example: amazon.com/orders routes to the Orders service Target Group; amazon.com/cart routes to the Cart service Target Group — via one ALB.

terms.definition: An Application Load Balancer feature that routes requests based on the domain name in the Host header, allowing different subdomains to reach different backends.
terms.example: orders.company.com routes to Target Group A; payments.company.com routes to Target Group B — via one ALB.

terms.definition: The rule ASG uses to decide which instance to terminate when scaling in. The default balances Availability Zones first, then selects the instance using the oldest launch template.
terms.example: When scaling in from 6 to 4 instances, ASG first picks the AZ with the most instances, then terminates the one running the oldest launch template version.

terms.definition: The ASG instance lifecycle state when a new EC2 instance is being launched but is not yet healthy or serving traffic. Health checks are not evaluated during the grace period for Pending instances.
terms.example: When ASG launches a replacement for a failed instance, the new instance enters Pending state while it boots up.

terms.definition: The ASG instance lifecycle state when an instance is healthy and actively receiving traffic from the Load Balancer. This is the normal operating state.
terms.example: After booting and passing health checks, an instance transitions from Pending to InService.

terms.definition: A mechanism that pauses an instance in a Wait state (Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait) during launch or termination, allowing custom scripts or workflows to run before the action completes.
terms.example: Use a Terminating:Wait lifecycle hook to drain a database connection pool before the instance is permanently terminated.

terms.definition: An individual rule within a Step Scaling policy that defines the scaling amount for a specific range of metric values.
terms.example: Step adjustment: when CPUUtilization is between 70 and 85%, add 2 instances.

terms.definition: A logical grouping of backend targets (EC2 instances, IP addresses, or Lambda functions) that a Load Balancer routes traffic to. Each target group has its own health check configuration.
terms.example: A microservices architecture uses one Target Group per service — all behind a single ALB with path-based routing rules.
